standing: Finite construction selections for required method families. Source metadata and scoped previews identify the intended treatment; full technical acquisition/reading and writing remain explicit tasks. No findings or proofs are accepted from abstracts.

methods.title: Entropy and the information represented by a distribution
methods.question: What does entropy measure, and which transformations preserve its interpretation?

sources.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
sources.version: The 55-page corrected reprint identifying the 1948 Bell System Technical Journal papers; not silently identified with the later 1949 book
sources.extent: Sections 6 and 20 in full, with every proof dependency for their stated properties; source's own appendix references must be followed. Preserve discrete versus continuous scopes.

components: Define the event/distribution, logarithmic units and entropy functional on its actual domain
Present the characterization and finite joint/conditional entropy properties with full required proofs
Present the selected continuous entropy properties and coordinate dependence with integrability assumptions
Separate statistical information amount from semantic truth, evidential support and decision value
Work a discrete dependence comparison and a change-of-coordinates boundary
prerequisites: P15-U1 finite probability, integration and conditioning
methods.success: Compute the named quantities under explicit assumptions and justify each claimed invariant or inequality.
methods.failure: Density entropy is treated as coordinate independent or entropy is treated as truth or utility.

methods.title: Relative information, divergence and sufficiency
methods.question: How does a distributional comparison quantify discrimination, and what does data reduction preserve?

sources.title: On Information and Sufficiency
sources.authors: S. Kullback and R. A. Leibler
sources.version: 1951 original article, Annals of Mathematical Statistics 22(1)
sources.extent: Complete original article and its stated information/sufficiency results; primary locator was reached but yielded only a container, so body acquisition and metadata verification remain due.

components: Define the compared probability measures, support and absolute-continuity conditions
Derive the selected information inequalities with all equality conditions
Reconstruct the source's relation to sufficient statistics and data reduction
Distinguish directed divergence from a distance, posterior probability and expected utility
Give support-mismatch, asymmetry and information-loss cases
prerequisites: P15-U1 Radon-Nikodym densities, integration and conditional expectation
methods.success: Every comparison and reduction theorem states and uses its exact measure and finiteness hypotheses.
methods.failure: A divergence is used as an unqualified metric or a missing support condition is hidden.

methods.title: Maximum-entropy inference under declared constraints
methods.question: What distribution does an explicit information constraint select, and what licenses that selection?

sources.title: Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics
sources.version: Physical Review 106, 1957, original first paper; the separate sequel is not merged
sources.extent: The complete maximum-entropy construction and inferential argument in the original paper, including its constraint/normalization derivations and stated statistical-mechanical application boundaries.

components: State the sample space, constraint functions and feasible distributions
Derive the optimizer and its existence/uniqueness qualifications
Explain multipliers and normalization without assuming a feasible optimizer exists
Reconstruct the normative inferential argument and its premises
Work a changed-constraint or reference-measure example separating mathematical optimization from evidential warrant
methods.success: The worked distribution solves the declared optimization problem and the inferential interpretation remains conditional on its stated premises.
methods.failure: An optimization result is treated as unconditional scientific truth or coordinate/reference choices disappear.

methods.title: Inference by minimum description length
methods.question: How do model and data coding costs select a statistical description?

sources.title: Modeling by shortest data description
sources.extent: Complete original 1978 article, including structure/parameter description, estimates and qualifications; later MDL variants remain distinct if separately selected.

components: Specify observed sequence, model family and parameter representation
Define total code length and the model-selection objective
Reconstruct the source's structural and numerical parameter estimation argument
Expose coding precision, parameterization and model-class dependence
Compare with the existing Occam PAC theorem using a case that separates their guarantees
methods.success: The selected model minimizes the specified description criterion and its guarantee is not confused with a different learning theorem.
methods.failure: Description length is an undefined complexity penalty or is equated with posterior truth or universal generalization.

methods.title: Imprecise probability and lower-prevision reasoning
methods.question: How can incomplete probability judgments be represented and updated without inventing a single precise distribution?

sources.title: Imprecise Probabilities
sources.version: Wiley StatsRef republication, 29 September 2014; publisher identifies its 2006 Encyclopedia of Statistical Sciences origin separately
sources.extent: Complete identified article and the exact lower-prevision/coherence/conditioning dependencies needed to supply its selected method; cited monographs are not automatically full-book obligations.

components: Define lower/upper probability and prevision objects and their consistency requirements
Relate a coherent assessment to its compatible probability set under explicit assumptions
Specify update and extension operations including zero-lower-probability boundaries
Separate lower previsions, belief functions and possibility measures
Work a decision comparison retaining imprecision and identifying required independence assumptions
methods.success: The represented bounds and updates have declared semantics and the comparison with precise probability is justified.
methods.failure: Unlike scales or evidence-combination assumptions are silently identified.

methods.title: Computations as decisions with costs
methods.question: When should an agent think further rather than act?

sources.title: Principles of Meta-Reasoning
sources.version: KR 1989 conference presentation, printed 400-411; the 1991 Artificial Intelligence article is a distinct presentation
sources.extent: Complete KR 1989 paper. The separately located CMU Newell-archive PDF contains only one page and cannot satisfy acquisition.

components: Define external actions, computational actions, time/space costs and information states
Construct the computation-utility model from changes to external decisions
Reconstruct exact and approximate solution conditions and their limitations
Address the source's philosophical and practical objections to evaluating unperformed computations
Calculate a stopping/continuation case and compare ideal optimization with a feasible policy
methods.success: The selected computation has justified expected benefit relative to its declared cost and information state.
methods.failure: The cost of reasoning about the computation or uncertainty about its outcome is omitted.

methods.title: Generated quantitative reasoning and its evidential standing
methods.question: What does successful language-model problem solving establish about a particular answer?

sources.title: Solving Quantitative Reasoning Problems with Language Models
sources.version: arXiv:2206.14858v2, 1 July 2022; v1 dated 29 June is separately identifiable
sources.extent: Complete selected v2 paper and appendices, preserving exact tasks, models, prompting, sampling, evaluation and error analyses.

components: State generation inputs and the actual task/evaluation protocol
Separate final-answer correctness from a sound derivation
Describe training, prompting, sampling and selection assumptions
Present the dated task-specific evidence and error boundaries
Work a human verification procedure for the exact question, assumptions, calculations and conclusion
methods.success: Every performance claim is dated and scoped, and a particular answer's justification is checked separately.
methods.failure: Benchmark accuracy or a fluent explanation is treated as a proof or as a claim about all current models.

methods.title: Premise retrieval and checked proof search
methods.question: How can retrieved mathematical premises guide proof search without becoming a substitute for proof?

sources.title: LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
sources.version: NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks published paper
sources.extent: Complete proceedings paper and its included appendices; exact benchmark/split, premise extraction, retrieval, tactic search and checking assumptions.

components: Separate informal target, formal theorem, proof state and available library premises
Reconstruct premise extraction and retrieval interfaces
Explain tactic generation/search and failure outcomes
State checker, axioms, library and formalization trust boundaries
Interpret the dated empirical evaluation without equating a checked formal theorem to an unverified informal target
methods.success: The retrieved premise is applicable and the actual formal proof checks under disclosed assumptions, with the informal/formal correspondence justified.
methods.failure: Retrieved relevance or search success for a different theorem is credited as the intended proof.

methods.title: Model self-evaluation and calibration
methods.question: What can a model's reported confidence tell a user about answer correctness?

sources.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
sources.version: arXiv:2207.05221v4, 21 November 2022; earlier July versions remain separate
sources.extent: Complete selected v4 paper and appendices, including task formats, calibration estimates, self-evaluation variants and transfer limitations.

components: Distinguish answer-conditioned correctness confidence from knowing-an-answer predictions
Specify elicitation format and score/calibration measures
Reconstruct the actual evaluation and sample-selection protocol
Analyze generalization to new tasks and dependence on supplied context
Give a case separating confidence, calibration and verification of an individual argument
methods.success: Reported confidence is interpreted under its measured task/format conditions and uncertainty.
methods.failure: A calibrated aggregate or self-evaluation score is treated as proof of a particular answer.

methods.title: Questions, measurement and design of an inquiry
methods.question: Which design can answer a stated empirical question, and which assumptions limit that answer?

sources.title: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions
sources.version: Selected chapter-specific 6.5/6.5.1 manifestations at the 7 September 2026 cutoff; exact chapter update dates must accompany capture
sources.extent: Chapters 2-6 for question/eligibility/search/data/effect-measure methods, and the exact design dependencies in chapters 8 and 23 used by this unit; record chapter-specific dates because the site mixes update years.

components: Define question, target population, estimand and operational measurements
Specify eligibility, sampling, assignment and data-collection rules
Distinguish random error, selection, measurement bias and confounding
Construct a design and derive what it can establish
Work a case where a different measurement, sampling or assignment mechanism defeats the conclusion
methods.success: The inference follows from the stated design and its assumptions, with portability beyond the source's intervention-review context justified.
methods.failure: A study's existence or a generic evidence checklist substitutes for an identified design and conclusion.
methods.scope_question: Pin chapter-specific pre-cutoff versions for the selected design dependencies; a current URL alone does not settle this source-version choice.

methods.title: Combining compatible evidence and representing heterogeneity
methods.question: When do estimates from different studies support a meaningful combined conclusion?

sources.title: Analysing data and undertaking meta-analyses
sources.authors: Jonathan J. Deeks, Julian P. T. Higgins, Douglas G. Altman, Joanne E. McKenzie and Areti Angeliki Veroniki, editors
sources.version: Cochrane Handbook chapter 10, version 6.5, last updated November 2024; the current page and version history retain this chapter-specific identity
sources.extent: Sections 10.1-10.14, with the formula/method dependencies actually used; preserve fixed/common-effect, random-effects, effect-measure, heterogeneity, dependence, missing-data and sensitivity distinctions.

components: Decide compatibility of estimands, designs and outcome scales before pooling
Derive the selected weighted-estimate procedures and their uncertainty assumptions
Distinguish common-effect estimation, heterogeneous effects and prediction
Handle dependence, incompatible estimates and missing information explicitly
Work a combined estimate and a case in which pooling or a subgroup comparison misleads
methods.success: The synthesis answers a specified shared question and its dependence/heterogeneity assumptions constrain the conclusion.
methods.failure: Evidence is double-counted or an average of incompatible effects is presented as new certainty.

methods.title: Missing evidence and selective reporting
methods.question: How can unavailable studies or outcomes bias a synthesis?

sources.title: Assessing risk of bias due to missing evidence in a meta-analysis
sources.authors: Matthew J. Page, Julian P. T. Higgins and Jonathan A. C. Sterne
sources.version: Cochrane Handbook chapter 13, version 6.5, last updated August 2024
sources.extent: Sections 13.1-13.4, including the missing-evidence distinctions, mitigation, ROB-ME process and its interpretive boundaries; cited empirical studies are selected as exact dependencies for examples actually used.

components: Separate missing studies, results and outcome definitions
Explain how selective availability changes the observed evidence set
Specify search/registry/protocol and inception-cohort strategies with limitations
Reconstruct the selected risk-of-bias assessment and sensitivity reasoning
Give a case separating funnel asymmetry from proof of publication bias
methods.success: The assessment identifies the missing-evidence mechanism and its uncertainty without overstating a diagnostic signal.
methods.failure: Only published favorable findings are treated as the complete corpus or asymmetry is assigned a unique cause.

methods.title: Sequential collection and stopping of evidence
methods.question: Which error guarantees survive a data-dependent stopping rule?

sources.title: Sequential Tests of Statistical Hypotheses
sources.version: Annals of Mathematical Statistics 16(2), June 1945, 117-186; later reprints remain distinct
sources.extent: Complete original selected test construction, stopping/error and sample-size arguments; exact primary capture/extent must be verified before writing. Relate separately to the existing Huber 1965 robust sequential treatment.

components: Define continuation and terminal decisions with their information sets
Construct the selected likelihood-ratio rule and boundaries
Prove claimed stopping/error guarantees under all stated assumptions
Explain finite/unbounded sampling and any approximations
Compare a valid sequential design with repeated use of a fixed-sample threshold
methods.success: The guarantee applies to the actual selection/stopping procedure.
methods.failure: A fixed-sample error statement is asserted unchanged after unplanned repeated inspection.

methods.title: Program synthesis from partial implementations and specifications
methods.question: How can examples and counterexamples guide a search for an implementation that satisfies a finite specification?

sources.title: Combinatorial Sketching for Finite Programs
sources.authors: Armando Solar-Lezama, Liviu Tancau, Rastislav Bodik, Vijay Saraswat and Sanjit Seshia in the located paper's displayed order
sources.version: ASPLOS 2006 original paper, 404-415; author bibliography orders the last two authors differently, so preserve and resolve that manifestation detail at intake
sources.extent: Complete identified final paper, including sketch language, synthesis/verification loop, finite-program correctness/completeness limits and evaluation. Bibliographic order discrepancy does not change the selected full paper extent.

components: Specify holes, partial program, finite input domain and desired behavior
Reconstruct the combinatorial synthesis and counterexample/verification interfaces
Prove the selected finite-domain correctness and completeness claims with their assumptions
Separate a fitted example set from a verified universal finite specification
Trace success, unrealizable specification and resource-exhaustion cases
methods.success: The synthesized program satisfies the exact specification under the stated finite-domain semantics.
methods.failure: Agreement on a sample or a bounded check is asserted as an unrestricted program theorem.

methods.title: Multiplicity and sequentially rejective testing
methods.question: How can a family of tests control false rejection under explicit dependence assumptions?

sources.title: A Simple Sequentially Rejective Multiple Test Procedure
sources.extent: Complete original article, including rule, error-protection proof, power comparisons and applications.

components: Define the hypothesis family, valid p-values and familywise error event
State and derive the step-down rejection rule
Prove protection for every configuration of true hypotheses
Compare with unadjusted and Bonferroni testing
Work a multiple-comparison failure and its remedy without adding an independence premise the proof does not require
methods.success: The displayed procedure controls its stated family error criterion for the actual hypothesis configuration.
methods.failure: Single-test significance is applied to a selected family without multiplicity control.

methods.title: Uniform convergence and capacity-dependent generalization
methods.question: When can observed frequencies support uniform claims over a class of events?

sources.title: On the Uniform Convergence of Relative Frequencies of Events to Their Probabilities
sources.authors: V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis
sources.version: Theory of Probability and Its Applications 16(2), 1971, 264-280; SIAM English presentation, online 17 July 2006, distinct from the earlier 1968 Russian paper
sources.extent: Complete selected 1971 presentation and every named theorem/construction used for the uniform-convergence treatment; preserve measurability and sampling hypotheses.

components: Define event-class complexity and the uniform discrepancy
Reconstruct the source's finite-sample estimates and limiting criteria
State all measurability and independent-sampling conditions
Derive the selected learning consequence from the actual convergence result
Contrast finite-class guarantees, high-capacity failure and distribution shift
methods.success: The bound is calculated under every stated hypothesis and its uniform domain is explicit.
methods.failure: Training fit or a pointwise limit is promoted to a uniform generalization guarantee.

methods.title: Likelihood estimation and its theoretical conditions
methods.question: What does a likelihood-based estimate establish, and under which model and sampling assumptions?

sources.title: On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics
sources.version: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, Series A, 222, 1922, 309-368; author archive provides two source parts
sources.extent: Complete original paper's estimation, information and sufficiency presentation, retaining all stated and necessary regularity qualifications; later asymptotic reformulations are explicitly separate if needed to repair a claim.

components: Define statistic, estimand, likelihood and sampling model
Distinguish identification, consistency, efficiency and sufficiency
Reconstruct the selected estimation arguments with exact regularity conditions
Compare likelihood, confidence and posterior statements
Work nonidentification, boundary and misspecification failures with direct corrections where a source claim overreaches
methods.success: Each estimate and theorem has explicit model, sampling and regularity scope.
methods.failure: Maximizing a function is treated as a complete inferential guarantee or missing regularity is hidden.

methods.title: Inference to the best explanation and its rivals
methods.question: Under what assumptions can explanatory considerations warrant an inference?

sources.title: Inference to the Best Explanation
sources.version: Second edition, Routledge, 2004, ISBN 9780415242035; distinct from the 1991 first edition
sources.extent: Introduction, chapters 1-11 and conclusion as the complete selected argument; source-specific definitions, examples, objections and Bayesian comparison remain separate from Hempel-Oppenheim and empirical preference studies.

components: Reconstruct the accounts of induction, explanation and the causal model
Present IBE and contrastive inference with their premises
Analyze the raven paradox and Bayesian abduction comparison
Reconstruct explanatory guidance, loveliness/truth and prediction/prejudice arguments
Present objections, replies and a worked rival-explanation/defeater case
methods.success: The inferential recommendation follows conditionally from the declared standards and the relevant objections are addressed.
methods.failure: Explanatory preference or persuasive narrative is treated as deductive entailment or as established truth.
